warmup.q: A label helper reads when (event) { is ParcelCollected -> "pickup"; is ParcelDelivered -> "drop-off"; else -> "other" }. A teammate adds ParcelLost to the sealed ParcelEvent interface and ships. What happens to lost parcels?
options: The build fails until the helper handles ParcelLost
They are labelled "other", and nothing tells anyone
The helper throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException when the program runs
Kotlin adds a branch for the new type automatically
warmup.why: The else branch matches anything, including types that didn't exist when it was written, so the compiler has nothing to report. Without the else, the same change is a compile error at this very line. NoWhenBranchMatchedException only appears when a subtype compiled later reaches a when that was exhaustive when it was compiled.

opening:
Remember Pedal Post, the bike courier in the small town of the Design patterns track? Its riders carry parcels across town on cargo bikes, each with a handheld scanner. Scan a parcel at a door, and the scanner sends a short message to Pedal Post's program: parcel PP-7781, collected, 2,500 grams. Three parts of the program want to hear it. The tracking page adds a line, the load board adds the weight to the bike, and the sender gets a text.

That message is an event, a note that something already happened. The easy trap is to hand the scanner's raw text to every listener, so that each one reads and checks it for itself. The first test never notices: test scans are always tidy.

The Advanced Kotlin track ended with compiler plugins. Now Part 3 goes to work on one small library, in three sittings. In this one, we'll list every kind of parcel event as a closed set of types and give ids and weights types of their own. Then we'll check each scan once, at the door. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a rider's scanner and three handlers that each read its raw text, one of which tripped over 2.5. Now every kind of event is a box on one closed form, and ids and weights carry their units. One clerk at the door turns each scan into a typed event, or a note saying why not.

Now look in your own code for a Map<String, String> of raw fields handed to more than one function. Each of those functions is a handler reading raw fields.

Next, we'll build the bus that carries these events to the tracking page, the load board and the text sender. How does one handler sign up for every kind of event at once?

sections.h: What we'll build: an event library for a bike courier, starting with the model
sections.html:
Over three sittings, we'll build one small library, a piece of code that other parts of a program call. It's an event library. One part of a program announces that something happened, and other parts react, without the announcer knowing who is listening. The scanner code says "PP-7781 was collected" once. The tracking page, the load board and the text sender each hear it and do their own job. "Typed" means the compiler knows exactly which kind of event each one is, so a handler written for deliveries can never be handed a failed delivery by mistake. And everything happens inside one running program, with no network in between.

The three sittings build the library from the inside out. This one writes the model: the types for every event Pedal Post's program can see. The next one builds the bus, the part that carries each event to everyone who signed up for it. It's the board of bells from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus, grown up. The last one gives the library an API, the set of functions its callers use, that reads well from Kotlin and from Java. Each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any sitting.

Let's start with what goes wrong without a model. The demo has three handlers, small functions that each react to a scan, and each one reads the scanner's raw fields for itself. Here is the heart of the load board:

Java
static void loadBoard(Map<String, String> fields) {
    if ("collected".equals(fields.get("type"))) {
        long grams = Long.parseLong(fields.get("grams"));     // parsing, deep inside a handler
        onTheBikeGrams += grams;
    }
    // ... and the same for "delivered", with a minus
}
Kotlin
fun loadBoard(fields: Map<String, String>) {
    if (fields["type"] == "collected") {
        val grams = fields.getValue("grams").toLong()          // parsing, deep inside a handler
        onTheBikeGrams += grams
    }
    // ... and the same for "delivered", with a minus
}

Three scans go in, and the demo printed:

tracking collected PP-7781
load     +2500 g, on the bike: 2500 g
tracking delivered PP-7781
load     -2500 g, on the bike: 0 g
tracking collected PP-7782
FAILED   java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "2.5"
texts sent: 0

Two bugs came out of three scans. The third scan says "grams": "2.5", because the rider weighed that parcel in kilograms. The scanner sent it exactly as typed. It always does; the scanner has no opinions. So the load board threw NumberFormatException halfway through its job, and by then the tracking page had already told the world that PP-7782 was on a bike. And no text went out at all, because the text handler compares the type with "deliver", one letter short, and nothing ever complains. Each handler parses and checks for itself, so each one can fail in its own way, and the compiler can't see any of it.

The fix comes in three pieces, one per section, and Part 3 has already given us each one. A closed list of event types, so the compiler knows every case: the form with a fixed set of boxes to tick, from Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check. Small types for ids and weights, so a bad value can't even be built: the units on numbers from Value classes and what they compile to. And one function at the door that copies each scan onto the right form, or hands back a note saying what was wrong: the clerk at the door from Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla. Behind that door, no handler ever reads a raw field again.

Before you run the demo, predict which scan fails, in which handler, and how many texts go out.

sections.h: A sealed interface lists every kind of parcel event
sections.html:
Here is the model. Each event is a fact about one parcel, named in the past tense, and that naming is a decision. Observer and Command put requests on order slips, "restock rye bread, 12 loaves", which can wait, be done or be crossed out. An event is a different kind of paper. It says something already happened, so a handler can't refuse it, only react to it.

Java
sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover {
    ParcelId parcelId();
}
record ParcelBooked(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent {}
record DeliveryFailed(ParcelId parcelId, FailReason reason) implements ParcelEvent {}

sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered {
    Weight weight();
}
record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover {}
record ParcelDelivered(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover {}
Kotlin
sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId }
data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent
data class DeliveryFailed(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val reason: FailReason) : ParcelEvent

sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val weight: Weight }
data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover
data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover

Read it from the top. A sender booked a pickup, and nothing has moved yet. A delivery failed, with a reason such as NOBODY_HOME. And a handover is the moment a parcel passes from one pair of hands to another: collected from the sender, or delivered at the door.

sealed closes the list of direct subtypes, the types that implement an interface or extend a class directly. Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check pictured it as a request form with a fixed set of boxes to tick. In Kotlin, the subtypes must sit in the same package and the same module, the set of files the compiler builds together; Java names them after permits. Each leaf is a data class in Kotlin and a record in Java: a final class that holds its values and compares by them. Its properties are vals of types that never change, so an event is like a page in the printed recipe book of Immutable data and a functional core: a correction is a new edition, made with copy(), never a crossing-out. That matters in lesson 2, where every handler gets the very same object. So every branch of the tree ends at a leaf, except Handover, which is sealed again one level down. That middle level is a decision we'll use in lesson 2: a handler for Handover will hear about collections and deliveries, and nothing else.

The payoff is the exhaustive when: a when, or a Java switch, with a branch for every subtype and no else. The compiler checks it against the list, the way the clerk in Pattern matching with switch and record patterns worked down a printed sheet with one line per box:

Java
static boolean changesHands(ParcelEvent e) {
    return switch (e) {
        case Handover h -> true;                  // one case covers both leaves
        case ParcelBooked b -> false;
        case DeliveryFailed f -> false;
    };
}
Kotlin
fun changesHands(e: ParcelEvent): Boolean = when (e) {
    is Handover -> true                           // one branch covers both leaves
    is ParcelBooked, is DeliveryFailed -> false
}

Now a new kind of event arrives. Parcels get lost now and then, and nobody plans for it, which is exactly why the compiler should. Add ParcelLost to ParcelEvent, and every such when stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is ParcelLost' branch or an 'else' branch. State and Chain of Responsibility said it about an order's states: the compiler writes your to-do list. An else throws that list away. The new event quietly takes the else branch wherever nobody went back to look, and the demo's label function files every lost parcel under "other".

A sealed type with no else turns a new case into a list of compile errors. Leave the else out.

One gap stays open when the program runs. Exhaustiveness is checked when a file is compiled. If code compiled against the old model meets a ParcelLost built by newer code, Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException and Java throws MatchException. In our library that can't happen by surprise, because events arrive as raw fields and pass the door first. An old program refuses the unknown type there, as the last section shows.

In the demo, uncomment ParcelLost and predict which of the three functions stop compiling.

sections.h: Value classes give every number its unit
sections.html:
Look at this parcel: RawParcel("PP-7781", 40, 2500). Is it 40 grams and 2,500 centimetres long, or the other way round? The demo's RawParcel takes two Longs, so a swapped call compiles, and the program believes in a 40-gram parcel 25 metres long. Value classes and what they compile to started at the print shop's parcel desk, where every number carries its unit: 500 sheets, 2,500 grams. A value class, a class that wraps exactly one value and is a type of its own to the compiler, puts that unit into code:

Java
record ParcelId(String value) {
    ParcelId {
        if (!value.matches("PP-[0-9]{4,12}"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid parcel id: '" + value + "'");
    }
}
record Weight(long grams) {
    Weight {
        if (grams < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("weight must not be negative: " + grams);
    }
}
Kotlin
@JvmInline
value class ParcelId(val value: String) {
    init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid parcel id: '$value'" } }
    override fun toString(): String = value
    companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("PP-[0-9]{4,12}") }
}

@JvmInline
value class Weight(val grams: Long) {
    init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must not be negative: $grams" } }
    override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg"
}

Now ParcelCollected(Weight(2_500), ParcelId("PP-7781")) fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Weight', but 'ParcelId' was expected. And because init runs on every construction, a ParcelId that exists is a valid one: PP- and 4 to 12 digits. Nothing downstream needs to check it again.

You may wonder what all these small types cost. Very little, for the reason that lesson gave. Where a value class is used as itself, the compiler erases it to its one field. That's the print shop's back room, where the units are gone and the machines see plain numbers. The demo prints the fields of ParcelCollected through Java reflection, the JDK's way of asking a class about itself, and they are a java.lang.String and a long. The Java records are separate objects on the heap, the memory where objects live: one for each id and one for each weight. The Kotlin ones become objects too in the places that lesson listed, such as a List<ParcelId>, a nullable Weight? or a generic T.

The one-field rule made a decision for this model. A value class holds one field until Project Valhalla arrives, so a Weight is whole grams, and the unit lives in the type's name. That suits Pedal Post, which weighs everything in grams. If a partner courier ever reports pounds, the door converts them, and nothing behind it sees a pound. Lesson 3's design review comes back to that choice.

Weight also adds and subtracts, which the load board in lesson 2 will need. plus uses Math.addExact, which throws ArithmeticException instead of wrapping round to a negative number. minus needs no check of its own: a result below zero is a negative Weight, and the constructor already refuses those.

In the demo, uncomment the swapped constructor call and read both errors. Then compare the field types the Kotlin and Java versions print.

Both versions print refused: invalid parcel id: '7781' and refused: weight must not be negative: -500. sections.h: Check each scan once, at the door, then trust the types
sections.html:
The model refuses bad values, but bad values still arrive. The scanner sends what the rider typed, a partner's program sends what it likes, and a row in a database may have been fixed by hand. So one function turns raw input into the model, in one place, at the edge of the program: the line where outside data comes in. Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla pictured it as a clerk at the door who copies each letter onto the right form, or sends it back. Our clerk never throws:

Java
static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) {
    try {
        String type = field(fields, "type");
        return switch (type) {
            case "collected" -> new Ok(new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(field(fields, "parcelId")), weight(fields)));
            // ... one case per type
            default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'");
        };
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return new Rejected(e.getMessage());     // a reader or a constructor said no
    }
}
Kotlin
fun parseEvent(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed {
    // field(name) and weight() are small local readers that throw IllegalArgumentException
    return try {
        when (val type = field("type")) {
            "collected" -> Parsed.Ok(ParcelCollected(ParcelId(field("parcelId")), weight()))
            // ... one branch per type
            else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'")
        }
    } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
        Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event")  // a reader or a constructor said no
    }
}

Parsed is a small sealed type of its own, with two cases: Ok holds a valid event, and Rejected holds the reason a scan was refused. Notice what parse does not do. It doesn't check the tracking number's format or the sign of the weight. It calls ParcelId(...) and Weight(...) and turns their refusal into a Rejected. The rules live in the constructors, once. A second copy of them in the parser would drift the first time someone edits one and not the other. And parseEvent is a recipe card in the sense of Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on: the same fields always give the same result, and nothing outside it changes, so the lab tests it with plain maps and no setup at all.

Why return a result instead of throwing? Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either had two cooks. One hands back a note, "the custard split, let's serve cream", and the other throws the pan across the room. An exception is the thrown pan. The code that reads scans has to decide what a bad scan means, and an exception decides for it: it flies out of the reading loop, and the loop stops at the first bad scan. A Rejected is the note. The loop can set the scan aside with its reason, count it, and carry on with the next one. Don't retry it, though: a malformed scan stays malformed, however often you read it.

Behind the door, code trusts the types. A function that takes a ParcelCollected has a valid tracking number and a positive weight, because no other kind of ParcelCollected can exist. There is no !!, no toLong() and no if (type == ...) in any handler you'll write in lesson 2.

The door protects us from the future too. When Pedal Post adds ParcelLost, a program that hasn't been updated yet still parses raw fields with its old parser. A lost scan lands in its else branch and becomes Rejected("unknown event type: 'lost'"), and nothing crashes. That's why the edge is the one when that keeps its else. It's a when over strings, and strings can never be listed in full, so the lab's tests do the checking there instead.

Parse once, at the door, into an event or a note. Behind the door, trust the types.

The demo's parser knows only collections and deliveries. Predict which of its six scans are rejected, and for what reason, before you run it.

code.title: EdgeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l01.demo.edge @JvmInline value class ParcelId(val value: String) { init { require(Regex("PP-[0-9]{4,12}").matches(value)) { "invalid parcel id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value } @JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long) { init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must not be negative: $grams" } } override fun toString(): String = "$grams g" } sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val event: ParcelEvent) : Parsed data class Rejected(val reason: String) : Parsed } /** The edge: raw fields in, a model value or a reason out. It never throws. */ fun parse(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed { fun field(name: String) = fields[name] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("missing field '$name'") fun weight(): Weight { val raw = field("grams") return Weight(raw.toLongOrNull() ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("grams is not a whole number: '$raw'")) } return try { when (val type = field("type")) { "collected" -> Parsed.Ok(ParcelCollected(ParcelId(field("parcelId")), weight())) "delivered" -> Parsed.Ok(ParcelDelivered(ParcelId(field("parcelId")), weight())) else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event") // a constructor or a reader said no } } fun main() { val inbox = listOf( mapOf("type" to "collected", "parcelId" to "PP-7781", "grams" to "2500"), mapOf("type" to "collected", "parcelId" to "PP-7782", "grams" to "2.5"), mapOf("type" to "delivered", "parcelId" to "7781", "grams" to "2500"), mapOf("type" to "delivered", "parcelId" to "PP-7781", "grams" to "-500"), mapOf("type" to "collected", "parcelId" to "PP-7783"), mapOf("type" to "failed", "parcelId" to "PP-7784", "reason" to "NOBODY_HOME"), ) var accepted = 0 for (fields in inbox) { when (val p = parse(fields)) { is Parsed.Ok -> { accepted++; println("OK ${p.event}") } is Parsed.Rejected -> println("REJECTED ${p.reason}") } } println("$accepted accepted, ${inbox.size - accepted} rejected") }

alt.title: EdgeDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l01.demo.edge; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; public class EdgeDemoJava { record ParcelId(String value) { ParcelId { if (!value.matches("PP-[0-9]{4,12}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid parcel id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Weight(long grams) { Weight { if (grams < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("weight must not be negative: " + grams); } @Override public String toString() { return grams + " g"; } } sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered {} record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent {} record ParcelDelivered(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Rejected {} record Ok(ParcelEvent event) implements Parsed {} record Rejected(String reason) implements Parsed {} static String field(Map<String, String> fields, String name) { String v = fields.get(name); if (v == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing field '" + name + "'"); return v; } static Weight weight(Map<String, String> fields) { String raw = field(fields, "grams"); try { return new Weight(Long.parseLong(raw)); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("grams is not a whole number: '" + raw + "'"); } } /** The edge: raw fields in, a model value or a reason out. It never throws. */ static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) { try { String type = field(fields, "type"); return switch (type) { case "collected" -> new Ok(new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(field(fields, "parcelId")), weight(fields))); case "delivered" -> new Ok(new ParcelDelivered(new ParcelId(field(fields, "parcelId")), weight(fields))); default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'"); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a constructor or a reader said no } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Map<String, String>> inbox = List.of( Map.of("type", "collected", "parcelId", "PP-7781", "grams", "2500"), Map.of("type", "collected", "parcelId", "PP-7782", "grams", "2.5"), Map.of("type", "delivered", "parcelId", "7781", "grams", "2500"), Map.of("type", "delivered", "parcelId", "PP-7781", "grams", "-500"), Map.of("type", "collected", "parcelId", "PP-7783"), Map.of("type", "failed", "parcelId", "PP-7784", "reason", "NOBODY_HOME")); int accepted = 0; for (Map<String, String> fields : inbox) { switch (parse(fields)) { case Ok ok -> { accepted++; System.out.println("OK " + ok.event()); } case Rejected r -> System.out.println("REJECTED " + r.reason()); } } System.out.println(accepted + " accepted, " + (inbox.size() - accepted) + " rejected"); } }

try.expect: One scan passes and five are rejected: grams is not a whole number: '2.5', invalid parcel id: '7781', weight must not be negative: -500, missing field 'grams' and unknown event type: 'failed'. The tracking number and the sign were refused by the constructors, not by the parser. With your failed branch the last line reads 2 accepted, 4 rejected.

aside.title: What if the scans come through a message broker?
aside.html: Real programs often get their events from a message broker, a separate program that keeps messages until other programs read them; Kafka and RabbitMQ are well-known ones. The edge is then the loop that reads each message, and it calls parseEvent once per message. A Rejected goes to a separate queue kept for refused messages, often called a dead-letter queue, with its reason attached, and the loop moves on. Webhooks, calls that another company's program makes into yours, and rows read back from a database are edges too. Each gets one parse function, and nothing behind it handles raw fields.

compare.title: The event model in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Model.java (Java 21)
java.html: record ParcelId(String value) { ParcelId { if (!value.matches("PP-[0-9]{4,12}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid parcel id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Weight(long grams) { Weight { if (grams < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("weight must not be negative: " + grams); } @Override public String toString() { return BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg"; } } sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { ParcelId parcelId(); } record ParcelBooked(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent { ParcelBooked { if (weight.grams() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("booked weight must be positive: " + weight); } } record DeliveryFailed(ParcelId parcelId, FailReason reason) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { Weight weight(); } record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover { /* same check */ } record ParcelDelivered(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover { /* same check */ } static String summary(ParcelEvent e) { return switch (e) { // no default case ParcelBooked(var id, var weight) -> id + " booked, " + weight; case DeliveryFailed(var id, var reason) -> id + " not delivered: " + reason; case ParcelCollected(var id, var weight) -> id + " collected, " + weight; case ParcelDelivered(var id, var weight) -> id + " delivered, " + weight; }; }

kotlin.title: Model.kt
kotlin.html: @JvmInline value class ParcelId(val value: String) { init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid parcel id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("PP-[0-9]{4,12}") } } @JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long) { init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must not be negative: $grams" } } override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg" } sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId } data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent { init { require(weight.grams > 0) { "booked weight must be positive: $weight" } } } data class DeliveryFailed(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val reason: FailReason) : ParcelEvent sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val weight: Weight } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover { /* same check */ } data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover { /* same check */ } fun summary(event: ParcelEvent): String = when (event) { // no else is ParcelBooked -> "${event.parcelId} booked, ${event.weight}" is DeliveryFailed -> "${event.parcelId} not delivered: ${event.reason}" is ParcelCollected -> "${event.parcelId} collected, ${event.weight}" is ParcelDelivered -> "${event.parcelId} delivered, ${event.weight}" }

compare.note: Both versions have the same shape: sealed interfaces for the kinds, final carriers for the leaves, the checks in the constructor, and one exhaustive switch per operation. Three things differ. Kotlin's value classes compile to a String and a long wherever they're used as themselves, while Java's ParcelId and Weight records are separate objects until value records arrive with Valhalla. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them within one file), while Kotlin requires them to share the package and module. And a data class's copy() runs init, so collected.copy(weight = Weight.ZERO) throws: a new edition of the form goes past the clerk again, and records have no copy at all. kotlinc also writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does, so Java code can switch exhaustively over this Kotlin model, which lesson 3 relies on.

drill.title: Write the hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write the sealed hierarchy from memory: ParcelEvent, the sealed Handover and the four leaves (plain String ids and Long grams are fine). Then write changesHands(e) with no else, using one branch for Handover. Finally, add ParcelLost and say which of your functions must change.

answer.html: sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: String } data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: String, val grams: Long) : ParcelEvent data class DeliveryFailed(override val parcelId: String, val reason: String) : ParcelEvent sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val grams: Long } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: String, override val grams: Long) : Handover data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: String, override val grams: Long) : Handover fun changesHands(e: ParcelEvent): Boolean = when (e) { is Handover -> true is ParcelBooked, is DeliveryFailed -> false } // ParcelLost : ParcelEvent breaks changesHands (add `is ParcelLost -> false`). // A when over Handover alone would still compile.

alt.html: sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { String parcelId(); } record ParcelBooked(String parcelId, long grams) implements ParcelEvent {} record DeliveryFailed(String parcelId, String reason) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { long grams(); } record ParcelCollected(String parcelId, long grams) implements Handover {} record ParcelDelivered(String parcelId, long grams) implements Handover {} static boolean changesHands(ParcelEvent e) { return switch (e) { case Handover h -> true; case ParcelBooked b -> false; case DeliveryFailed f -> false; }; } // ParcelLost (added to permits) breaks changesHands: add `case ParcelLost l -> false;`.

recap: Handlers that read raw fields each parse and check for themselves, so a bad scan fails deep inside one of them after others have already acted on it.

A sealed interface closes the list of event types: Kotlin subtypes share its package and module, and Java names them in permits. A sealed middle level such as Handover lets one branch stand for its leaves.
Write every operation as a when or switch with no else, so a new event type becomes a compile error at each place that must handle it.
Value classes give ids and weights their own types at no cost where they're used as themselves, and their init blocks make every instance valid. One field only, so a Weight is whole grams.
Parse once, at the door, into the model. Return Ok or Rejected, never throw, and let the constructors make the checks. Behind the door, trust the types.
Where today's model stops: it describes events, and nothing delivers them yet. The tracking page, the load board and the texts still can't hear a scan; lesson 2 builds the bus.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why handlers take a ParcelCollected instead of the scanner's Map<String, String>: "the map has everything, and it's one less type to maintain." Explain what the sealed model and the door buy you, using a bug you could get with the map.
explain.answer: With the map, every handler parses and checks for itself. A scan that says "2.5" grams throws inside the load board after the tracking page already listed it, and a typo like "deliver" silently never matches. The model closes the list of event types, so a when without else lists every place that must change when a type is added. Value classes make a swapped id and weight a compile error, and their constructors make every instance valid. The door parses each scan once and returns Ok or Rejected, so a bad scan is set aside, with its reason, before any handler acts. Behind it, a handler that takes a ParcelCollected knows it has a valid tracking number and a positive weight. The extra types cost a few lines, and they remove a whole family of bugs that only show up on the day a rider types kilograms.

deeper.html:
Three questions come up once a model like this runs for real.

How do events change over time? Adding a field with a default is safe for programs that parse at the door: old scans lack the field and get the default. Renaming a type or a field is not. Keep the old name in the parser for as long as old scans can arrive, and map it to the new type there, so the model itself never carries the history. If you turn the model into JSON with kotlinx.serialization, as Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization showed, pin each type's name with @SerialName for the same reason.

Should the door return Either instead of a sealed Parsed? The Either<String, ParcelEvent> from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus works, and it composes with map and flatMap. A dedicated Parsed reads better where it's used (is Parsed.Rejected), and it leaves room for a third case later, such as Ignored for event types a program deliberately doesn't handle. Kotlin's Result<T> is the wrong fit: its failure side is a Throwable, and a rejected scan is not an exception, as Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either argued.

What about the database? Rows you read back are untrusted input too. A column holding 'collected' and a nullable grams column are a raw map with a schema, and a migration or a fix made by hand can break them. Read rows through the same kind of edge function, or reuse parseEvent by turning each row into its map of fields.

Java has one tool here that Kotlin doesn't need: since JDK 21, a pattern switch can take case null explicitly. Kotlin rules null out at compile time by declaring the parameter non-nullable. Both end up with the same guarantee behind the door.
